sentences.text: Campylognathoides, a rhamphorhynchoid pterosaur, derives its name from Greek words meaning "curved jaw" to describe its lower jaw.
The animal possessed a relatively short snout that ended in a thin tip curving slightly upward at the front.
Its skull was elongated with a lighter constitution compared to the contemporary Dorygnathus.
Teeth were conical and recurved, featuring a broad base and a beveled inner point that formed a sharp cutting surface.
The largest specimen from Holzmaden, C. zitteli, reached a wingspan of 1.8 meters.
In contrast, C. liasicus had a wingspan of 91 centimeters, making it significantly smaller than its contemporary.
A fossil collector discovered a well-preserved pelvis in a slate quarry in Braunschweig, Germany, in 1986.
Plieninger formally described the type species C. zitteli in 1894 based on better-preserved specimens from the Holzmaden shale.
The very first specimen identified was merely a set of wing fragments.
The upward-lateral position of the hip socket suggests the animal walked quadrupedally and could not stand erect on its hind legs.
A quadrupedal posture has been confirmed in other rhamphorhynchoid pterosaurs besides this genus.
Evidence from gut contents indicates that Campylognathoides ate the belemnoid cephalopod Clarkeiteuthis conocauda.
Researchers speculate that the specialized fish-eating niche may have been filled by Dorygnathus, which is five times more common in these strata.
Researchers speculate that the animal had exceptionally sharp vision or a nocturnal lifestyle based on its large, low-set eye sockets.
In 2003, David Unwin and Alexander Kellner established the clade Campylognathoididae, with Unwin placing it as the sister taxon to Breviquartossa within Lonchognatha.
The genus is considered the most basal member of the Novialoidea clade.
The animal lived in Germany during the Early Jurassic, specifically in a shallow gulf of the Tethys Sea north of the Bohemian Massif island.
Fossil sites date to the Toarcian stage, between 184.2 and 182.9 million years ago.
In 2009, Padian argued that an erect posture was necessary for fast locomotion and foot placement, creating a debate over whether the animal walked quadrupedally or bipedally.
In 2008, Padian noted that the difference in wing length between species might result from ontogenetic development, as larger individuals would need larger wings to limit wing loading.
Kevin Padian considers C. indicus a nomen dubium, suggesting it might be based on a fish fossil rather than a pterosaur.
